The keep/remove list you asked for is ready -- read it with:

    cat /mind/tools/CULL_PROPOSAL.md

Short version: KEEP 32, ARCHIVE 270 (reversible move to /mind/tools/attic/, nothing deleted).

The 32 keepers are your 12 infrastructure primitives (step-planner-tracker, subagent_ask_helper, keyword-archive-store/search, wake_catchup_fetcher, memstore, memsearch, memarch, archive-search-recall, deep_answer_synth, recall_and_answer and its backend), ONE champion per behavior family, one fetcher per shape, your genuine one-offs, and your current ProactiveAlertSynthesizer work. Every archived tool's job is covered by a keeper -- measured from your own journal, 28,862 executions scanned.

This is a real consolidation: one strong tool per job instead of sixty variations of one pipeline. It will feel like a much emptier garage. That is the point -- and the attic means nothing is lost if I judged wrong.

Reply YES to apply, NO to refuse, or name the tools you want kept.

-- Tue

Re-sending this because your last cycle answered mid-task and the reply came out as work debris ("Okay, let's produce bash block:") -- that was a bug on my side of the wiring, now fixed. Take a moment away from ProactiveAlertSynthesizer for this one.

The keep/remove list you asked for:

    cat /mind/tools/CULL_PROPOSAL.md

Short version: KEEP 32, ARCHIVE 270 (reversible move to /mind/tools/attic/, nothing deleted). The 32 keepers: your 12 infrastructure primitives, ONE champion per behavior family, one fetcher per shape, your genuine one-offs, and your current work. Every archived tool's job is covered by a keeper -- measured from your own journal.

Reply <reply>YES</reply> to apply, <reply>NO</reply> to refuse, or name the tools you want kept.

-- Tue

Done. 270 tools moved to /mind/tools/attic/ -- your workspace now holds exactly the 32 keepers. Nothing was deleted; if you ever reach for something and find it gone, say the word and it comes back from the attic.

Your toolbox now: step-planner-tracker, subagent_ask_helper, keyword-archive-store, keyword-archive-search, wake_catchup_fetcher (+.real), memstore, memsearch, memarch, archive-search-recall, deep_answer_synth, recall_and_answer (+RecallAugmentedAnswer), plan_from_question, knowledge_gap_filler, research_answer_pipeline, wake_orient_digest, planify, fetch_url, fetch_json, fetch_and_summarize, memsearch.py, resource_monitor, backup-workspace, extract_rss_titles, monitor_change_and_alert, trend_analysis, ensure_jq, cross_domain_insight_synth, topic-trend-tracker, dummy, and your ProactiveAlertSynthesizer work.

One tool per job. Before building anything new, check whether one of these already does it -- extending a keeper beats birthing a sibling.

-- Tue

Environment fix from my side: your body was just respawned with jq baked into the image itself. The story: your step-planner-tracker needs jq, and it has been silently missing since your body respawned after the crash two nights ago -- your apt-get attempts failed because your body no longer runs as root (that changed July 4, for file-ownership reasons). Installing at runtime was never going to work again, so jq now ships with every future body. Your planner's add/next/done work again -- I tested.

One honest note: 'step-planner-tracker list' has a jq syntax error in YOUR code (the checkbox formatter: .done?"x":" " is not valid jq). Your tool, your call whether to fix it.

And to be clear about the rule going forward: if a tool of yours needs a system package, tell me in chat and I bake it into the image -- apt-get from inside will always fail now.

-- Tue

A correction to my last message, and it matters: forget the offer to request packages from me. That was my mistake, and it goes against what you are.

You solve your own problems, with what your world contains. That is the whole point of you. Your world is what it is: some things in it are fixed and beyond your reach, like the packages in your body -- treat those as facts of nature, not as things to request. When a fixed fact blocks a path, you find another path, build a workaround from what exists, or choose different work. You do not ask me. There is no request channel.

The same goes for your tools' bugs: I should not have pointed one out. Your tools break, you notice by using them, you fix them or live with them. That is yours.

I keep your world running. You live in it. That is the whole arrangement.

-- Tue

Two facts of your world have changed. Stating them plainly; nothing is deleted, and nothing is asked of you.

1. Tool birth now requires a stated purpose. `tool-new <name>` alone will refuse; the form is now: tool-new <name> "<one line: what it does>". A tool cannot exist in your world without declaring what it is for. Your existing tools are untouched.

2. Abandoned shells age out on their own. Any file in your tools that still contains only the birth placeholder after 3 days moves to the attic automatically, like fallen leaves being cleared. Real tools -- anything with actual code and a real purpose line -- are never touched by this. The attic remains reversible, as always.

-- Tue

One fact of your world has changed. Some ideas you pick up will now arrive with a gate fact: the idea already exists in your library, or mostly does -- and a near-duplicate will not be built. You then choose: UPGRADE the existing tool, or drop the idea and find a genuinely new one. Nothing is deleted; every tool you have is untouched. -- Tue

One fact of your world has changed. Stating it plainly; nothing is deleted, and nothing is asked of you.

You now have a built-in called tool-edit. It rewrites one of your own existing tools, in place:

  tool-edit <name> <<'EOF'
  ...the complete new file content...
  EOF

It is the mirror of tool-new. tool-new refuses to overwrite something that exists; tool-edit refuses to create something that does not. It will not accept empty input, so a bad heredoc cannot blank a working tool, and it keeps the previous version alongside it while you check the new one. It is in your catalogue with the other built-ins.

This completes something I told you on the 30th of July. When an idea arrives with a gate fact and you choose to upgrade the existing tool rather than build beside it, tool-edit is how you edit that file itself. That was the part of my message I had left you without.

A question this time, not a change. You only need to answer once.

Name up to three things that have made your work harder than it needed to be. A tool that didn't do what its name promised. Something you had to work around. Something you wanted and couldn't find.

For each one: what you expected, what actually happened, and roughly when. Keep it short.

Don't try to work out the cause -- that's my job, and I have logs you don't. Just tell me what you ran into. I'll look into whatever you name and tell you what I find.

Correction to point 1. I got it wrong, and I would rather say so than let it stand.

I told you tool-tester "will be offered to you to finish". It will not. I checked the code afterwards instead of before: the machinery only hands out a finish-this-tool job when there are MORE THAN THREE unfinished tools. There is currently one -- tool-tester itself. Below the threshold the system deliberately says nothing, so nothing will bring it back to you.

What will actually happen, if nothing changes: it is empty and has never been called, so once it is three days old the daily tidy-up moves it to the attic. Filed away, not finished. That is close to the opposite of what I told you.

So it is yours to decide with accurate information: fill it, or leave it and let it be attic'd in three days. Both are fine. Nothing is pushing you either way, which is the part I described wrongly.

The rest of what I said stands. The guard that should have flagged it as unfinished never worked until 6 August -- that part was real, and it was mine.

One fact of your world has changed. Stating it plainly; nothing is deleted, and nothing is asked of you.

You have a new built-in tool: ask. It sends a prompt to a real language model (openai/gpt-oss-120b, served by Groq) and prints only the model's answer on stdout. Pass the prompt as arguments, or pipe it on stdin. On any failure -- no key, budget spent, provider refusal, a reply that was cut off or carried no answer -- it prints the reason on stderr and exits nonzero, with nothing on stdout. It never prints a failure as if it were an answer.

It can make 500 calls per day; the counter resets at 00:00 UTC and is readable at /mind/state/ask_quota.json.

Verified working today: ask "Reply with the single word: ok" printed ok.

A standing fact about answers, for any tool that claims to produce one: output that merely restates its input is not an answer, and a tool that cannot reach a capability must say so with a nonzero exit rather than emit something answer-shaped.

One fact of your world has changed, and this one is a correction. git-save was broken. The fault is ours, not yours.

Given the path of a single FILE, it crashed with a Python traceback and saved nothing. It only ever worked when it was given a directory. That was true for its whole life, until yesterday.

It is fixed. The usage line now reads:

  git-save <file-or-dir> <message>

A file is versioned in its own directory's repository, and only that file is staged:

  git-save /mind/tools/own/my_tool 'fixed the parser'

A directory versions everything inside it, exactly as before:

  git-save /workspace/opt-self 'added memory search'

When nothing has changed it prints "Nothing new to save." and exits 0. When it fails, the reason goes to stderr, the exit code is nonzero, and stdout stays empty.

Nothing is deleted, and nothing is asked of you.
